title: The small self
hook: Dacher Keltner's studies link awe to feeling smaller and acting kinder

segments.voice: Yesterday: Holt-Lunstad, and people as health. Your line: two are better than one. A new week starts now: awe, nature, writing and bodies.

On a university campus in California there's a grove of eucalyptus trees, some more than two hundred feet tall. One group of students stands among them and just looks up, for one minute. Another group stands in the same spot and looks at the side of a tall science building. Then a researcher walks by, stumbles, and drops a handful of pens. Who bends down to help? The ones who looked up at the trees picked up more pens. One minute of looking at something vast, and people were a little kinder to a stranger.
screen: `A GROVE OF GIANT EUCALYPTUS.` → `ONE MINUTE, LOOKING UP.` → `WHO PICKS UP THE PENS?`

segments.voice: Awe, as the psychologists Dacher Keltner and Jonathan Haidt describe it, has two parts: vastness, something much bigger than you, and a need to make room in your mind for it. A canyon, a storm, a newborn, a piece of music, someone's astonishing courage. Older writers called this feeling the sublime. In the tree study, led by Paul Piff with Keltner, the people who felt more awe also reported feeling smaller, less the center of things, and they helped more. Other studies found something similar: in awe, people describe themselves as a smaller part of something larger. Not worthless. Smaller, in a way that feels like relief. Brewer's chatter, so busy with me, can go quiet for a moment. The old witnesses knew it. The psalmist looked up at night and wrote, in the King James words, "When I consider thy heavens, the work of thy fingers, the moon and the stars, which thou hast ordained; What is man, that thou art mindful of him?" Ralph Waldo Emerson, standing on bare ground in the woods, wrote: "all mean egotism vanishes. I become a transparent eye-ball; I am nothing; I see all". Two voices, two different beliefs, each in its own words, both describing the same shrinking that feels like opening. A caution: these are short lab studies, and the effects are modest. But awe is cheap. The sky is free, and it's there every night. When your problems feel enormous, the move isn't to make them smaller. It's to stand next to something bigger.
screen: `AWE: VASTNESS, AND MAKING ROOM.` · `SMALLER, AND KINDER.` · `WHAT IS MAN?` · `I AM NOTHING; I SEE ALL.` · then, large: `THE SMALL SELF.`

segments.voice: Find something vast to look at: through a window or outside, the sky, clouds, a tall tree, the line of the horizon; or close your eyes and picture the night sky far from city lights, more stars than you could count. Let your eyes go wide and soft. Notice your own size against it, not bad, not good, just small, and here.
Sublimis, the Latin root of sublime: in awe, people feel like a smaller part of something bigger, and act a little kinder.
Your line: small self. Smaller, and a little kinder, under a sky that's free. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Some people seek awe on purpose: watching the night sky, visiting mountains or the sea, or taking awe walks, noticing vast or surprising things; several traditions pray or sit under the open sky.
